extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research-evaluation professionals, and science policy makers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and synthesis about evaluating scientific work using peer review, bibliometrics, and research impact assessment, and about designing fair, transparent assessment systems. Focus is on the strengths and limitations of common evaluation mechanisms and on alternatives that support research quality and integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of science evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Science evaluation is currently fulfilled through mechanisms of peer review, bibliometrics, and research impact assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter treats these three as the principal mechanisms for judging and validating scientific work and notes that each has limitations. Use this tripartite framing when diagnosing or designing evaluation systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness of peer review
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical work shows ways in which peer review can be unfair and how it might be improved. Evaluation systems should therefore diagnose sources of unfairness (bias, status effects, network influence) and adopt reforms supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of evaluation processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Science evaluation should be conducted in a fair and transparent manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency is presented as a core desideratum for any trialed alternative evaluation approach; systems should make criteria, procedures, and decisions visible to stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding overreliance on citation counts
rubrics_metrics.description: The widespread use of citation counts in decisions about scientific quality is undermining science’s ability to meet its core mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation counts should not be treated as a sole or dominant proxy for quality because their use can damage the community’s ability to self-regulate. Consider complementing or replacing raw citation metrics with richer, contextualized indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for science’s core mission and research quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation should support science’s basic purposes and standards of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment systems must prioritize whether they help produce and recognise work that meets disciplinary quality standards rather than merely optimising metric scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial and evaluation of alternative approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an urgent need to trial approaches to science evaluation which better serve to support its basic purposes in a fair and transparent manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and institutions should pilot new evaluation methods (and evaluate those pilots) rather than assuming established metrics are adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarding against gaming and metric manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Gaming science indicators (e.g., excessive self-citation, citation stacking) undermines metric validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment frameworks must include protections and detection for gaming behaviours and consider incentive effects of chosen metrics; the references document instances of manipulation and sanctioning (e.g., journals denied impact factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor, transparency, and trustworthiness of research methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of rigor and transparency (for example, the rigor and transparency index; Ripeta score) are relevant quality metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality-assessment tools that quantify methodological rigor, reporting transparency, and trustworthiness are discussed as alternatives or complements to citation-based indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring societal and translational impact responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments of research impact should consider societal and translational outcomes and equity (e.g., societal impact frameworks, inclusion-immediacy criterion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact assessment must be methodologically careful and attentive to which stakeholders benefit; the literature contains frameworks and critiques for mapping and measuring societal impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and inter-reviewer agreement in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review and grant-review judgments can show low agreement; questions about how many reviewers are required for reliable evaluations arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of review processes should consider empirical evidence on reviewer agreement and the number/selection of reviewers needed to achieve acceptable reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-specific notions of research quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-existing notions of research quality mean that understandings of 'good research' are context-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation systems should be sensitive to discipline- and context-specific logics; a single universal metric is unlikely to capture all relevant dimensions of quality.
